passage_text: Researchers at the University of Health Sciences conducted a pilot study to evaluate the efficacy of a novel antihypertensive agent, Hypertensol, in reducing systolic blood pressure (SBP). Twenty adult volunteers with mild to moderate hypertension were enrolled and randomly assigned to receive either Hypertensol (n=10) or a placebo (n=10) for four weeks. Baseline SBP was measured after a 5‑minute seated rest using an automated cuff. After the treatment period, SBP was reassessed under identical conditions. The investigators recorded the change in SBP for each participant and performed a paired t‑test to determine statistical significance. The following table lists SBP values for five of the ten Hypertensol patients (P1–P5). These five patients show a mean reduction of 11 mmHg, with the largest individual drop observed in patient P5. While the study demonstrates potential benefit, limitations such as the small sample size and short duration warrant cautious interpretation.
table_data:
Patient ID | Baseline SBP (mmHg) | Post-treatment SBP (mmHg) | Change (mmHg)
P1 | 120 | 110 | -10
P2 | 140 | 130 | -10
P3 | 130 | 125 | -5
P4 | 150 | 140 | -10
P5 | 160 | 140 | -20
stem: Which patient experienced the greatest reduction in systolic blood pressure?
explanation: Patient P5’s SBP decreased from 160 to 140 mmHg, a 20‑mmHg drop, which is larger than any other patient’s reduction.
trap: Option A is tempting because P1 also had a 10‑mmHg drop, but it is not the greatest.

stem: Which feature of this pilot study most limits conclusions about the drug’s effect?

options.A: Random assignment of patients to drug or placebo
options.B: A 5‑minute seated rest before measuring SBP
options.C: The small sample (n = 10 per group) and short duration (four weeks)
options.D: Use of an automated cuff under identical conditions

explanation: Correct: The passage itself notes that the small sample size and short duration warrant cautious interpretation. Why the others are wrong: A) Random assignment reduces bias and is a strength. B) A standardized rest period reduces measurement variability. D) Identical measurement conditions reduce variability.
trap: Treating randomization or standardized measurement procedures as flaws; they are strengths, whereas the small sample and short duration limit conclusions.

stem: What is the mean change in systolic blood pressure across the five patients listed in the table?
explanation: Correct: (−10 − 10 − 5 − 10 − 20)/5 = −55/5 = −11 mmHg. Why the others are wrong: A) −5 mmHg is the smallest single change (P3). C) −15 mmHg does not follow from the five listed changes. D) −20 mmHg is the largest single change (P5).
trap: Picking −20 mmHg (option D), the single largest change, or −5 mmHg (option A), the smallest, instead of averaging all five changes.

stem: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the data?

options.A: All five listed patients had a lower SBP after treatment.
options.B: The greatest reduction was observed in patient P5.
options.C: The average reduction among the five listed patients was 11 mmHg.
options.D: The drug had no effect on patient P3.

explanation: Correct: D) P3 fell from 130 to 125 mmHg, a 5 mmHg reduction, so this statement is contradicted. Why the others are wrong: A) All five changes are negative. B) P5 fell 20 mmHg, the most. C) The mean of −10, −10, −5, −10 and −20 is −11 mmHg.
trap: Reading a small change of 5 mmHg as no effect; any fall in SBP is a reduction, even though the table alone cannot attribute it to the drug.

stem: Which of the following best describes the relationship between baseline systolic blood pressure and the magnitude of reduction observed?

options.A: Higher baseline SBP tended to be associated with a larger reduction in these five patients.
options.B: Lower baseline SBP is associated with a greater reduction.
options.C: There is no association between baseline SBP and reduction.
options.D: Only patients with baseline SBP >150 mmHg experienced a reduction.

explanation: Correct: A) The 160 mmHg patient had the largest fall (20 mmHg) and the correlation across the five patients is positive (r about 0.7), though five patients is too few to be conclusive. Why the others are wrong: B) The lowest-baseline patients did not have the largest falls. C) There is a positive trend. D) Patients with baseline below 150 mmHg also fell.
trap: Option D is incorrect because patients with baseline <150 mmHg also showed reductions.
